Vitamin D may have a role in anti-TB immunity through activation of macrophages (Cegielski and McMurray, 2004; Cegielski
and Vernon, 2015). Induction of a cell-surface receptor for the vitamin D metabolite, 25-hydroxycholecalciferol, as well as the
hydroxylase which forms 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, appear to be part of the mechanism that helps these cells destroy the
pathogen. These vitamin D effects are linked with production of the endogenous antibiotic peptide, cathelicidin. Two cross-
sectional studies on vitamin D metabolism in relation to TB have focused on the molecular and cellular mechanisms of the
interaction rather than on the direction of causality (reviewed in Cegielski and McMurray (2004)). Cells recovered by bron-
choalveolar lavage (BAL) and peripheral blood mononuclear cells from TB patients both produced 1,25(OH)2D3, the amount
correlating with the number of CD8þ T lymphocytes but not with other cell types. CD4þ T lymphocytes in BAL ﬂuid from TB
